{"id": "30:60/q04", "question": "What does 'do not let them yastakhiffannaka' mean?", "turns_on": "The root's lightness is applied to agitation or haste, and some glosses extend its effect to foolish error or departure from religion.", "positions": [{"id": "30:60/q04/p1", "position": "Do not let them unsettle, distress, agitate, or dislodge your steadiness.", "reasons": "Al-Azharī, as reported by al-Wāḥidī, names judgment and forbearance; al-Baghawī reports judgment and patience; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says remain unmoved despite lack of insight. Al-Nasafī cites what opponents say and do; al-Rāghib, via al-Bursawī, says their doubts must not dislodge belief. Al-Ālūsī mentions denial and abuse, including charges that messengers lie; Kur'an Yolu adds belittlement, doubt, and anxiety. Study Quran translates the verb 'disquiet.' Al-Iṣlāḥī describes the mockers as trying to uproot the Prophet, while the closing command assures him that they will fail."}, {"id": "30:60/q04/p2", "position": "Do not let them hurry or provoke you into haste or angry reaction.", "reasons": "Ibn Shajara gives 'make you hurry'; Yaḥyā 'provoke.' Al-Jushumī explains istikhfāf as seeking lightness: making a people light prompts haste, while overwhelming delight impairs judgment. Al-Jubbāʾī warns anger would violate patience and gentleness. Al-Nasafī mentions a premature request for punishment; Ibn ʿĀshūr says figurative lightness denotes panic or visible anger. Study Quran also gives rushing and unsteadiness."}, {"id": "30:60/q04/p3", "position": "Do not let them lead you into foolishness, error, or transgression.", "reasons": "Al-Azharī says istakhaffa can mean treating someone as foolish and inducing error; al-Baghawī gives that gloss as well as impaired judgment. Al-Qurṭubī says making someone foolish enough to follow error; Study Quran reports from Q a sense of making someone heedless or ignorant, leading to error and transgression."}, {"id": "30:60/q04/p4", "position": "Do not let them draw you down from your position or away from your religion.", "reasons": "Al-Naqqāsh gives the first gloss; al-Zajjāj and his later transmitters explain the warning as preventing opponents from provoking or unsettling the Prophet away from religion. Yaḥyā says he must not follow their call to abandon it."}, {"id": "30:60/q04/p5", "position": "Do not let them dismiss your views as flimsy and weak.", "reasons": "Al-Iṣlāḥī glosses istikhfāf as treating someone's views as flimsy and weak."}]}
{"id": "30:60/q05", "question": "How is yastakhiffannaka read?", "turns_on": "The variants change the root from istikhfāf to istihqāq, or change the emphatic nūn's weight while retaining the prohibition.", "positions": [{"id": "30:60/q05/p1", "position": "The common reading has khāʾ and fāʾ, from istikhfāf, with an emphatic heavy nūn.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya contrasts the majority form with istihqāq; al-Samīn derives it from istikhfāf. Al-Biqāʿī says its emphatic prohibition is stronger than a bare prohibition and guards the foundations of religion against conceding to opponents. Al-Ālūsī says the majority geminate the nūn. The Qirāʾāt note specifies a third-person plural subject."}, {"id": "30:60/q05/p2", "position": "The nūn is light or unvowelled, while the prohibition keeps its meaning.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the two alternative readers also transmit silent nūn in the istikhfāf form. Ibn al-Jawzī assigns sukūn to Yaʿqūb except Rawḥ and Zayd; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī assign it to Yaʿqūb. Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī name Ibn Abī ʿAbla and Yaʿqūb; Qirāʾāt says lightening reduces emphasis. Al-Nashr points to its earlier treatment of Ruways's reading at Āl ʿImrān."}, {"id": "30:60/q05/p3", "position": "An alternative reads yastaḥiqqannaka with ḥāʾ and qāf, from istihqāq.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya names Ibn Abī Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb; al-Samīn agrees. Al-Bayḍāwī glosses it as not letting opponents turn the addressee away. Al-Biqāʿī attributes it to Ruways from Yaʿqūb, connects ḥaqq with not oneself seeking a just settlement from opponents, and warns that worldly concessions invite demands for favoritism. Al-Ālūsī says not to let them win the addressee over until they are more entitled to him than believers; he applies this reading to the community because the Prophet is protected."}]}
{"id": "30:60/q06", "question": "How does the prohibition work grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:60/q06/p1", "position": "It is a prohibition with an emphatic nūn, formally directed at the opponents but functionally telling the Prophet not to be affected.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī say the jussive prohibition with heavy nūn is built on fatḥa. Al-Samīn compares the idiom 'do not let me see you here.' Al-Bursawī says the apparent ban on unbelievers indirectly forbids the Prophet from yielding to contempt; al-Ālūsī similarly invokes the idiom and glosses it as not grieving fearfully over them. Al-Biqāʿī says emphasis strengthens the ban beyond a bare prohibition."}]}
{"id": "30:60/q07", "question": "What is the case and form of alladhīna?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:60/q07/p1", "position": "Alladhīna is nominative; some Arabs use alladhūna in the nominative.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī state the case; al-Naḥḥās reports the Arab usage الذون, also given by al-Qurṭubī as اللذون."}]}
{"id": "30:60/q08", "question": "Who lack certainty, and what do they doubt?", "turns_on": "The sources variously locate the missing certainty in revelation generally, the afterlife, imminent worldly punishment, divine help, or the promise itself; al-Qurṭubī also reports a named individual.", "positions": [{"id": "30:60/q08/p1", "position": "They are unbelievers or polytheists who reject the Prophet's message and remain doubtful or astray.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā calls them polytheists urging the Prophet to leave his religion. Ibn ʿAbbās, as reported by al-Wāḥidī, says they disbelieve what the Prophet brought. Al-Wāḥidī's Abū Isḥāq calls them astray and doubtful; Ibn al-Jawzī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Bayḍāwī, and al-Bursawī give doubt, lack of insight, or denial of signs. Al-Ālūsī names their accusations that messengers lie; al-Biqāʿī includes wavering doubters."}, {"id": "30:60/q08/p2", "position": "They deny resurrection, judgment, or recompense.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī specifies deniers of resurrection; al-Māwardī offers this as an alternative to unbelievers generally. Al-Wāḥidī reports another interpretation; al-Baghawī and Ibn al-Jawzī mention resurrection and reckoning or recompense."}, {"id": "30:60/q08/p3", "position": "They doubt punishment will descend on them in this world.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī reports Muqātil's explanation and identifies these people as those punished at Badr."}, {"id": "30:60/q08/p4", "position": "They doubt divine support and confidently expected Persia to defeat Rome.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says their prediction risked their credibility because God had promised Roman victory; he also includes wavering doubters."}, {"id": "30:60/q08/p5", "position": "They are specifically al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports this identification. Muqātil elsewhere recounts al-Naḍr demanding immediate punishment and later being killed at Badr, with ʿAlī beheading him."}, {"id": "30:60/q08/p6", "position": "They are people who lack belief in God's promise itself.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī mentions this alternative only to dismiss it."}]}
{"id": "30:60/q09", "question": "Who receives the closing warning?", "turns_on": "The prophetic address can be taken as direct, extended to the community, or applied to the community particularly under the istihqāq reading.", "positions": [{"id": "30:60/q09/p1", "position": "It directly addresses the Prophet Muhammad.", "reasons": "Most explanations address his patience and steadiness amid opponents; al-Ālūsī says the prohibition, although formally cast with a plural subject, is directed to him."}, {"id": "30:60/q09/p2", "position": "The address to the Prophet also intends his community.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī says the warning is worded for him but intended for the community; Study Quran reports this interpretation from Q. Kur'an Yolu extends the closing encouragement to believers and callers."}, {"id": "30:60/q09/p3", "position": "On the istihqāq reading it addresses the community, because the Prophet is protected.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī explains that the alternate reading warns against opponents becoming more entitled to the addressee than believers."}]}
{"id": "30:60/q10", "question": "How does the conclusion connect to the sūrah's argument?", "turns_on": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī explicitly favors the sūrah-wide promise of victory over a reading centered on distress at rejected signs.", "positions": [{"id": "30:60/q10/p1", "position": "The close follows obstinate rejection and sealed hearts, so the Prophet must persevere.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī says God has just reported their sealed hearts. Ibn Kathīr cites the many examples given to clarify truth, the dismissal of signs as magic including the moon's splitting, and 10:96–97 on those who would not believe even after every sign. Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies the omitted object of patience as their obstinacy after 30:58. Al-Ālūsī and Study Quran likewise connect the exhortation to sealed hearts; al-Iṣlāḥī says only people of intellect receive the historical proofs in 46–60."}, {"id": "30:60/q10/p2", "position": "The close returns to the sūrah's promise of divine help and victory.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 30:47 and says the sūrah begins and ends with promised help; he rejects making distress at denied signs the main reason for the patience command. Al-Biqāʿī connects the Romans' promised victory, which exposed doubters' error, with the promised Hour's justice for wrongdoers and reward for the virtuous. Al-Iṣlāḥī reads 46–60 as historical proofs of help. Study Quran links the promise's truth to 30:6 and lists 4:122, 10:4, 10:55, 18:21, 28:13, 31:33, 35:5, 40:55, 40:77, 45:32

{"id": "30:60/q11", "question": "What happened when ʿAlī recited this verse in prayer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:60/q11/p1", "position": "A Kharijite insinuated ʿAlī's shirk by reciting 39:65 during dawn prayer, and ʿAlī answered with 30:60.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says Qatāda also transmits the episode. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says ʿAlī recognized the insinuation. Al-Ālūsī names Ibn Abī Shayba and others as transmitters and judges the response apt from the Prophet's brother and gate of the city of knowledge. Al-Māwardī, al-Durr, and al-Itqān likewise report the prayer exchange."}]}
{"id": "30:60/q12", "question": "What occasion involving al-Naḍr is reported?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:60/q12/p1", "position": "After al-Naḍr demanded immediate punishment, Muhammad was told not to be provoked; al-Naḍr was later killed at Badr.", "reasons": "Muqātil says ʿAlī beheaded al-Naḍr and the dead are displayed to the Fire morning and evening. Al-Wāḥidī transmits Muqātil's identification of doubters in worldly punishment with those punished at Badr; al-Qurṭubī reports naming al-Naḍr as the one lacking certainty."}]}
{"id": "30:60/q13", "question": "What other experiences illustrate endurance of opposition?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:60/q13/p1", "position": "After Abū Ṭālib died, abuse intensified; someone threw dust on the Prophet, and he assured his weeping daughter of God's protection.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī says the daughter wiped the dust from his head and adds that the Companions also endured abuse and ultimately prevailed."}]}
{"id": "30:60/q14", "question": "What is reported about reciting Sūrat al-Rūm in dawn prayer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:60/q14/p1", "position": "The Prophet stumbled during its recitation and attributed the confusion to some worshipers' poor ablution.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr reports his instruction to perform ablution well, grades the chain and text ḥasan, and infers that a follower's prayer is connected to the imam's."}]}
{"id": "30:60/q15", "question": "What virtue is reported for reciting Sūrat al-Rūm?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:60/q15/p1", "position": "The reciter receives ten rewards per angel praising God between heaven and earth, compensating for missed deeds by day and night.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī transmits this as a prophetic report."}]}
{"id": "30:60/q16", "question": "Was this verse abrogated?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:60/q16/p1", "position": "Some exegetes say it was abrogated.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī reports the claim without further argument in this note."}]}
{"id": "30:60/q17", "question": "May Qur'anic wording be used in other speech, as in ʿAlī's reply?", "turns_on": "The jurists differ over whether adapting Qur'anic wording into other expression is disliked or permitted.", "positions": [{"id": "30:60/q17/p1", "position": "Using Qur'anic expressions in poetry or other writing is permissible.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī states this without doubt in al-Itqān, alongside the report of ʿAlī answering a Kharijite with the verse during prayer."}, {"id": "30:60/q17/p2", "position": "Some jurists dislike making parables from Qur'anic wording.", "reasons": "Al-Itqān transmits this from al-ʿImād al-Bayhaqī through al-Ṣalāḥ."}]}
{"id": "30:60/q18", "question": "How does the Qur'an present proof to deniers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:60/q18/p1", "position": "It uses every kind of clear proof, argument, distinction, and warning in familiar Arab speech.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī says plain arguments convince ordinary listeners without obscure technical disputation while teaching specialists too; Ibn Abī al-Iṣbaʿ counters al-Jāḥiẓ's claim that kalām argument is absent from the Qur'an and defines such argument as evidence decisively defeating an opponent."}]}
{"id": "30:60/q19", "question": "How is the verse applied to seekers on the inward path?", "turns_on": "The inward notes apply patience both to enduring critics and to the seeker's own self-discipline and detachment.", "positions": [{"id": "30:60/q19/p1", "position": "Seekers must endure mockery from people who belittle the quest for God.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī says even holders of inherited faith may lack certainty, deny that seeking God is obligatory, and scorn those who leave worldly life, family, and children. Al-Ālūsī applies the warning to heirs of the Muhammadan way and spiritual guides whose states, words, and deeds are rejected by veiled deniers."}, {"id": "30:60/q19/p2", "position": "The seeker patiently detaches from worldly ties and inward attachment until the self gives way to union.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī gives outward detachment then inward separation from happiness in either world, citing 64:14 and the saying of two steps followed by arrival. He reports ʿAṭṭār's clod dissolving in the sea and the Mathnawī's grammarian and boatman: grammar cannot prevent drowning, whereas self-effacement lets the sea carry the dead. Najm al-Dīn defines patience as disciplining desire, guarding the heart from ego traits, and surrendering the spirit's separate existence to divine generosity; Ḥāfiẓ urges steadfast love because it is rewarded."}]}
{"id": "31:13/q01", "question": "Who was Luqmān?", "turns_on": "Reports about his status, occupation, appearance, and identification differ; Ibn ʿĀshūr weighs narrative wording and report chains.", "positions": [{"id": "31:13/q01/p1", "position": "He was a wise, pious man, not a prophet.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿUmar transmits a Prophetic description of a reflective, convinced servant loved by God and given wisdom. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites the majority and Mālik's title al-ḥakīm; the story mentions neither revelation nor angels and presents counsel rather than legislation."}, {"id": "31:13/q01/p2", "position": "He was a prophet.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima and al-Shaʿbī argue that wisdom can mean prophethood, as with David and 2:269; God's instruction concerning parents appears amid his counsel (31:14)."}, {"id": "31:13/q01/p3", "position": "He worked as a tailor.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib supplies this occupation."}, {"id": "31:13/q01/p4", "position": "He was flat-nosed and Abyssinian, or Black from Nubia or Abyssinia.", "reasons": "Qatāda gives the flat-nosed Abyssinian report; Hudhayl says he did not hear Muqātil transmit that description. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls reports of Blackness and Nubian or Abyssinian origin weak in chain."}, {"id": "31:13/q01/p5", "position": "The Qurʾānic Luqmān is distinct from Luqmān ibn ʿĀd and from Balaam.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the latter identifications arose from confusion about names, fathers, or translated names; Balaam is the figure of Numbers 22–23."}]}
{"id": "31:13/q02", "question": "What is the name of Luqmān's son?", "turns_on": "The transmitted names vary, with no criterion in these notes to settle them.", "positions": [{"id": "31:13/q02/p1", "position": "Anʿam or Anam.", "reasons": "Muqātil calls him Anʿum; Bursevī says Luqmān was known as Abū Anʿam. The slight vocalization differences are reported together."}, {"id": "31:13/q02/p2", "position": "Mishkam or Mashkam.", "reasons": "The minor spelling and vocalization forms are transmitted by al-Kalbī and other reports."}, {"id": "31:13/q02/p3", "position": "Thārān, Tārān, Dārān, Barān, or Tharan.", "reasons": "Al-Suhaylī attributes Thārān to al-Ṭabarī and al-Qutbī; al-Ālūsī reports Ṭabarī and Qutaybī as Tārān. The forms vary in transmission."}, {"id": "31:13/q02/p4", "position": "Ashkam.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī gives this form; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī list it alongside other reported names."}, {"id": "31:13/q02/p5", "position": "Bābān.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī lists this among the alternatives."}, {"id": "31:13/q02/p6", "position": "Mathān.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī lists this alternative."}]}
{"id": "31:13/q03", "question": "What was the son's religious state, and what became of him?", "turns_on": "Whether the warning addressed existing unbelief or prevented a future lapse, and how long the counsel continued.", "positions": [{"id": "31:13/q03/p1", "position": "He and Luqmān's wife were unbelievers and accepted Islam after repeated admonition.", "reasons": "Muqātil and later reports give the conversion; Bursevī contrasts Noah's son and wife and Lot's wife with Lot's believing daughters."}, {"id": "31:13/q03/p2", "position": "The son and wife were already Muslim; the warning guarded against future shirk.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this alternative."}, {"id": "31:13/q03/p3", "position": "Luqmān continued advising his son until the son died.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī cites al-Faḍl al-Raqqāshī."}]}
{"id": "31:13/q04", "question": "How was Luqmān's son described?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:13/q04/p1", "position": "He was described as barr, meaning beneficent or thankful.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān records both explanations of the descriptor."}]}
{"id": "31:13/q05", "question": "How does وَإِذْ relate to the preceding wording?", "turns_on": "Whether an omitted imperative, the earlier grant of wisdom, or an extra particle accounts for idh; al-Naḥḥās objects to the wisdom link on word order and the wāw.", "positions": [{"id": "31:13/q05/p1", "position": "An omitted command, 'remember,' governs idh.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī prefer the implied command; al-Naḥḥās rejects attachment to the grant of wisdom because of the intervening wāw and order. Al-Ṭabarī and others take God to tell Muḥammad to recall the counsel."}, {"id": "31:13/q05/p2", "position": "Idh attaches to God's giving Luqmān wisdom: the admonition was itself wisdom.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and Abū Isḥāq place the gift at the time of the couns

{"id": "31:13/q06", "question": "What is the syntax of وَهُوَ يَعِظُهُۥ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:13/q06/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause describing Luqmān as admonishing his son while speaking.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim, al-Samīn, and al-Ālūsī identify the ḥāl; al-Samarrāʾī infers sustained counsel and a receptive moment from the construction."}]}
{"id": "31:13/q07", "question": "What does waʿẓ mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether waʿẓ is characterized chiefly by warning or by a heart-softening reminder of good; Elmalılı expressly favors al-Khalīl's definition.", "positions": [{"id": "31:13/q07/p1", "position": "Admonition or deterrence joined to warning and rebuke.", "reasons": "Rāghib gives deterrence with warning or fear; Bursevī and al-Ālūsī repeat this sense."}, {"id": "31:13/q07/p2", "position": "A reminder of good that softens the heart.", "reasons": "Al-Khalīl's definition is cited by Bursevī and al-Ālūsī; Elmalılı judges it better. Al-Biqāʿī adds benefit, discipline, reverence, and justice."}, {"id": "31:13/q07/p3", "position": "Calling people to the Real and His way.", "reasons": "Sulamī transmits the definition from Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī. Ibn ʿAbbās says Luqmān's admonition concerns God."}]}
{"id": "31:13/q08", "question": "What manner and occasion of admonition does the wording suggest?", "turns_on": "The precise occasion is inferred by Iṣlāḥī; other notes draw continuity and care from the wording.", "positions": [{"id": "31:13/q08/p1", "position": "He gave sustained, careful counsel, with repeated attention to his son.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī hears repetition; al-Samarrāʾī takes the circumstantial wording as continuity and recommends ongoing parental guidance. Al-Ālūsī's mustard-seed story depicts many lessons and the son's tears. Iṣlāḥī sees a deliberate, elaborate occasion."}, {"id": "31:13/q08/p2", "position": "He counseled the son when the son was being crowned the next tribal chief.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī infers this specific occasion."}]}
{"id": "31:13/q09", "question": "Why use the diminutive address يَٰبُنَىَّ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:13/q09/p1", "position": "It expresses tenderness, love, and concern, making the son receptive to advice.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Biqāʿī, Bursevī, al-Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Asad say it need not mean literal youth or smallness; al-Ālūsī cites two poems. Al-Samarrāʾī likens gentle address to 20:44 and gives the example of a parent sitting beside a child and touching his head or shoulder; he favors gentle, noncoercive counsel and recounts his own son's response."}]}
{"id": "31:13/q10", "question": "How is يَٰبُنَىَّ formed grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:13/q10/p1", "position": "It is the diminutive of ibn with a possessive yāʾ, whose reduction explains the surviving final yāʾ and its vowel.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr describes restored and merged root letters and omission of the vocative possessive yāʾ. Al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī say kasra signals an omitted yāʾ and fatḥa eases pronunciation. Abū ʿAlī compares kasra to yā ghulāmi aqbil and fatḥa to an added yāʾ changed to alif, as in yā abati; al-Fārisī cites Abū ʿUthmān and compares possessive yāʾ to tanwīn. Al-Wāḥidī explains deletion after three yāʾs and treats an underlying final yāʾ as still present, citing poetry and the plural; he prefers other accounts of the lightening and says it better suits verse-ending rhyme. Qirāʾāt-ER calls the silent form shorter and compressed and the kasra form more explicitly possessive."}]}
{"id": "31:13/q11", "question": "How is the final yāʾ of يَٰبُنَىَّ read here?", "turns_on": "Transmission by reader and route, and whether a pause form may be sounded in connected speech.", "positions": [{"id": "31:13/q11/p1", "position": "With kasra and a doubled yāʾ.", "reasons": "The majority and named readers Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim use kasra; Ibn Kathīr has it in the middle occurrence. Al-Fārisī calls kasra the normal vocative after dropping the possessive yāʾ; Qirāʾāt-ER says it retains clearer possession."}, {"id": "31:13/q11/p2", "position": "With fatḥa and a doubled yāʾ.", "reasons": "Ḥafṣ and al-Mufaḍḍal from ʿĀṣim have fatḥa in the three Luqmān occurrences; Ḥafṣ has it throughout the Qurʾān. The underlying form is explained as yā bunayā with an elided or substituted alif; al-Fārisī and Abū ʿUthmān compare yā abati. {"id": "31:13/q16", "question": "What does ẓulm mean as an Arabic word?", "turns_on": "The word's range of Arabic usage; the explanations may coexist.", "positions": [{"id": "31:13/q16/p1", "position": "Putting something outside its proper place.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba gives idioms for resemblance, premature drinking, needless slaughter, wrongly dug land and leaving a road; al-Zajjāj and al-Wāḥidī state the same base sense."}, {"id": "31:13/q16/p2", "position": "Diminution or withholding.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba cites crops, rights, and souls in 2:57, 18:33, 19:60 and 36:54 for what is not diminished; al-Ṭabrisī applies withholding to God's due."}, {"id": "31:13/q16/p3", "position": "Denial.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba cites Thamūd's denial of the she-camel's divine origin and denial of God's signs in 17:59 and 7:9."}]}

{"id": "31:13/q26", "question": "Where and how many verses was Sūrat Luqmān revealed?", "turns_on": "Reported Medinan exceptions and verse-count systems; al-Ālūsī challenges the prayer-and-zakat dating argument.", "positions": [{"id": "31:13/q26/p1", "position": "It is wholly Meccan.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās gives this report."}, {"id": "31:13/q26/p2", "position": "It is Meccan except verses 31:27–29, revealed in Medina after a challenge by Jewish rabbis.", "reasons": "Another Ibn ʿAbbās report connects the exception to the comparison of human knowledge with the Torah."}, {"id": "31:13/q26/p3", "position": "It is Meccan except the two verses starting with the trees-and-pens parable.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ gives the report, also attributed by al-Dānī and Abū Ḥayyān to Qatāda."}, {"id": "31:13/q26/p4", "position": "A proposed Medinan exception is the verse about prayer and zakat.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports the argument that both obligations began in Medina, but objects that prayer was prescribed at the Meccan Night Journey and at least enjoined there; an alternative account distinguishes the Meccan obligation of zakat from Medinan thresholds."}, {"id": "31:13/q26/p5", "position": "Its verse count is thirty-three in Meccan and Medinan systems, thirty-four in other systems.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī records the counting difference."}]}
{"id": "31:13/q27", "question": "How does the sūra connect to the preceding sūras?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:13/q27/p1", "position": "It resumes themes and contrasts from preceding sūras: guidance, signs, wise conduct, pleasure, resurrection, and shirk.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī cites al-Baḥr on parables and rejected signs (29:43, 29:50, 31:7), al-Suyūṭī on shared opening letters and the believers of 29:49, and contrasts rejoicing in the garden (30:15) with idle song (31:6), Roman-Persian struggle for worldly prize with a wise enslaved man counseling patience and peace, two accounts of easy resurrection (30:27; 31:28), and responses to hardship and shirk (30:33; 31:32)."}]}

{"id": "31:13/q29", "question": "What other wisdom or counsel is attributed to Luqmān in reports accompanying this verse?", "turns_on": "Distinct transmitted sayings and episodes, rather than a dispute over one saying.", "positions": [{"id": "31:13/q29/p1", "position": "He gave detailed travel counsel about prayer, companions, rest, animals, food, safety, and conduct.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports Luqmān on praying promptly and in congregation, resting and feeding a mount, choosing grassy camps and praying on arrival and departure, giving food, reciting while riding, praising God, solitary prayer, avoiding all-night travel and loudness; Abū ʿAbdillāh adds gear, medicine, consultation, generosity, verifying advice, heeding elders and caution with lone strangers."}, {"id": "31:13/q29/p2", "position": "He likened the world to a deep sea: faith is the ship, trust its sail, and piety its provisions.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī attributes this to Man lā yaḥḍuruhu al-faqīh; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports al-Ṣādiq adding that many learned people perish, survival is mercy and drowning follows sin."}, {"id": "31:13/q29/p3", "position": "The heart and tongue are the best morsels

 when good and the worst when bad.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports Luqmān bringing them when his master asked for a sheep's two best morsels."}, {"id": "31:13/q29/p4", "position": "He warned against lingering on the toilet and described physical harm.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī says he named liver harm, hemorrhoids and head heat, advised gentle sitting and rising, and his master wrote it on the privy door."}, {"id": "31:13/q29/p5", "position": "He answered family deaths with statements about changed responsibility and loss.", "reasons": "ʿAbd Allāh ibn Dīnār reports Luqmān's reactions to his father, wife, sister and brother dying: control of his affairs, a renewed bed, covered nakedness and lost support."}, {"id": "31:13/q29/p6", "position": "The worst person is untroubled by being seen doing wrong.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports Luqmān's answer to a question."}, {"id": "31:13/q29/p7", "position": "He answered criticism of his face by asking whether it targeted the design or its designer.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports the exchange."}, {"id": "31:13/q29/p8", "position": "He praised David's armor and said silence is rare wisdom.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī says David affirmed that Luqmān deserved his name."}, {"id": "31:13/q29/p9", "position": "He urged nearness to scholars, restraint in the world, fasting desire, and keeping prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Ṣādiq says not to dispute scholars, take only enough from worldly life, and not let fasting desire obstruct prayer, which God loves more."}, {"id": "31:13/q29/p10", "position": "He urged sustained learning and avoidance of bad company and disputation.", "reasons": "Reports compare early manners to later fruit and knowledge to an inherited habit; they counsel daily learning, guarding knowledge, avoiding quarrels with obstinate people or jurists, hostile rulers, tyrants and the wicked. {"id": "31:13/q31", "question": "What broad interpretive principles are drawn from this verse and its use elsewhere?", "turns_on": "The notes present complementary interpretive principles.", "positions": [{"id": "31:13/q31/p1", "position": "Qurʾānic wording must be read for its intended scope and contextual meaning.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says not to narrow broad wording, broaden specific wording, or absolutize restricted wording; he explains the Qurʾān's guidance, legislation and ethical principles as concise and transmissible, allowing scholarly derivation, with 5:3 on completed favor.
